newsitem.title: FRANCE: French mediator to review immigrants' status.
newsitem.headline: French mediator to review immigrants' status.

text.p: French Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin named a mediator on Tuesday to look into the controversial issue of thousands of illegal immigrants seeking residence permits.

Jospin's office said Jean-Michel Galabert, a judge on the State Council, the country's top administrative court, would oversee a scrutiny of individual cases "pending re-definition of the current legal framework".

Government sources said the new left-wing government would instruct government officials across the country to grant the documents to immigrants fulfilling certain criteria -- possibly involving tens of thousands of people .
The move looked certain to raise an outcry on the right. Opinion polls show most French people want the hardline legislation to stay.

The mediator was appointed after Jospin met a group of African "sans papiers" (without papers) protesters who marched to Paris from the southwestern city of Angouleme to request residence permits that the previous conservative government had refused them.

Many of them Malians who have lived in France for years, they say they were deprived of residence rights by a stiffening of immigration laws by conservative ex-interior minister Charles Pasqua in 1993.

The left, which came to power in a parliamentary election 10 days ago, has vowed to repeal the hardline legislation which it says is contrary to France's tradition of hospitality and pandered to the far-right anti-immigrant National Front which wants to send all immigrants home.

The number of immigrants who could win residence rights under the review ordered by Jospin was unclear. The daily Le Monde put it at 20,000 to 40,000. A spokesman for the protesters said it would affect 100,000 people.

Government sources said those who would qualify for residency include parents of children born in France, spouses of immigrants with legal status, those who would be in danger if sent home, patients receiving extensive medical care, students, and immigrants "well-integrated in French society".
The immigrant issue sparked nationwide controversy last August when police stormed a church and forcibly evacuated some 200 Africans who had taken refuge there to avoid expulsion.
Magistrates later overturned orders expelling most of them.
Many "sans papiers" are in a legal limbo as they are unable to obtain residence rights but cannot be expelled for a variety of reasons -- including having children born in France.

Ex-interior minister Jean-Louis Debre pushed through earlier this year a law which was intended to close the legal loopholes but drew widespread protests by film-makers and academics for further clamping down on immigration.
There are an estimated five million foreigners in France, of whom about one million, mostly North Africans, are thought to be illegal.
